title: West Los Angeles
name: West Los Angeles
metaTitle: West Los Angeles in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for West Los Angeles office along the Olympic Corridor, Westwood medical suites, and Sawtelle-area retail and multifamily.

sections.html: West Los Angeles covers the office corridor running along Olympic Boulevard and Bundy Drive, plus the medical and small-retail streets closer to Westwood. It is a more varied market than Century City next door, mixing legacy professional office with a newer wave of technology tenants that expanded inland from the coast.

sections.heading: The Olympic Corridor's Office Stock
sections.html:
Office buildings along the Olympic Corridor were largely built for law firms, insurance offices, and other professional-services tenants in the 1980s and 1990s, and many now carry technology and media tenants that outgrew coastal office space and moved inland for larger floor plates. A buyer replacing into this corridor should model near-term capital needs for lobby, HVAC, and elevator upgrades on buildings of that vintage, since deferred maintenance is common on Class B stock that has cycled through several tenant types.

Parking ratios also vary more than buyers expect along this stretch, since some 1980s-era buildings were built to older, lower parking standards that newer technology tenants find tight once a floor is occupied at higher density. A rent roll that assumes an easy re-lease to a similar-sized tenant should be checked against the building's actual parking ratio, since a mismatch there can slow lease-up more than any cosmetic capital item.

sections.heading: Medical Office Demand Near Westwood
sections.html:
The medical office market bordering the Westwood medical corridor runs on a different demand driver than the rest of West Los Angeles, since physician groups and outpatient practices value proximity to Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center regardless of general office market conditions. Medical office buildings here carry higher build-out costs per suite, and a replacement buyer should confirm what portion of tenant improvement costs the current owner has already amortized before assuming a clean pro forma.

Lease structures on medical suites also tend to run longer than standard office leases, since a physician practice moving exam rooms and imaging equipment faces a real cost to relocate, and that stickiness is part of what makes this niche attractive to a replacement buyer coming out of a shorter-term retail or industrial hold. Confirming whether a specific suite is built for general practice or for a more specialized use, imaging or outpatient surgery in particular, matters because re-leasing costs differ sharply between the two.

sections.heading: Where Coastal Tenants Land Inland
sections.html: A former retail center on Pico Boulevard converted into large-floor-plate technology office is the most visible example of coastal tenant demand moving into West Los Angeles, and that shift has pulled office rents in the corridor closer to Santa Monica pricing than the corridor saw a decade ago. Replacement buyers should treat this as a market still adjusting rather than a fully settled comparable set, since sale pricing on office assets near this conversion has moved faster than pricing on comparable buildings a mile or two east.

sections.heading: The West Los Angeles Identification Set
sections.html:
Investors working a West Los Angeles list are usually choosing among:

  • Olympic Corridor and Bundy Drive Class A and B office buildings
  • medical office suites and small medical buildings near Westwood
  • Sawtelle-area small-format retail and restaurant buildings
  • garden-style apartment buildings on residential side streets bordering the office corridor

sections.heading: Positioning West Los Angeles on a Three-Property List
sections.html:
West Los Angeles works well as an anchor identification because its office and medical inventory is deeper than Century City's or Beverly Hills', giving a buyer more genuine alternatives if a specific building falls out of contract. A qualified intermediary coordinating a West Los Angeles closing should confirm the appraiser is pulling comparables from within the corridor rather than blending in Santa Monica or Century City pricing, since the three markets have moved at different speeds over the last several years.

A buyer with a shorter runway left in the 45-day identification window often favors West Los Angeles precisely because of that depth, since a fallen-through office deal here is more likely to have a genuine backup already sitting on the same identification list than a fallen-through Century City or Beverly Hills deal would.

faqs.q: How is West Los Angeles office different from Century City?
faqs.a: West Los Angeles has a deeper and more varied bench of buildings across several decades of construction, while Century City is a small, concentrated cluster of towers, which gives West Los Angeles buyers more genuine alternatives on an identification list.

faqs.q: Why does medical office near Westwood behave differently than the rest of the corridor?
faqs.a: Demand there is tied to proximity to Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center, so occupancy and lease renewal patterns can hold up even when general office conditions elsewhere in West Los Angeles soften.

faqs.q: Are technology tenants a meaningful factor in this submarket?
faqs.a: Yes. A number of larger-floor-plate technology tenants have moved into West Los Angeles from the coast, particularly around former retail sites converted to office use, and that shift has pushed rents in parts of the corridor closer to coastal pricing.

faqs.q: What should a buyer check before replacing into an Olympic Corridor office building?
faqs.a: Confirm the building's age-related capital needs, particularly HVAC, elevator, and lobby systems, since many corridor buildings date from the 1980s and 1990s and carry deferred maintenance from multiple tenant turnovers.

faqs.q: Does West Los Angeles have meaningful multifamily inventory for an exchange?
faqs.a: Some, mostly garden-style apartment buildings on residential streets bordering the office corridor, though the submarket is better known for office and medical space than for multifamily replacement product.
